Where it began

Curtly Ambrose was born on 21 September 1963 in the village of Swetes, on Antigua. As a boy he preferred basketball, did well at school in mathematics and French, and on leaving at 17 became an apprentice carpenter. Cricket came late. He shot up to 6 feet 7 inches in his late teens, and a good day bowling fast in a softball game persuaded him to try club cricket at 20.

A Viv Richards scholarship took him to England, where he took 84 wickets for Chester Boughton Hall in 1986 and 115 for Heywood the year after. Back home he became the Leeward Islands' spearhead, and by 1988 he was in the West Indies side.

The player

He played 98 Tests between 1988 and 2000 and took 405 wickets at 20.99, with 22 five-wicket innings. For much of his career he was ranked the world's leading bowler, first reaching the top of the rankings in 1991.

He had a gift for the match-turning spell. Against England in 1990, as the visitors tried to bat out the final hour, he took their last five wickets for 18 runs and finished with 8 for 45, his best figures. In Australia in 1993 his ten wickets in one Test helped West Indies to victory by a single run, and in the deciding Test he took seven wickets for one run in a spell of 32 balls. A year later in Trinidad he took 6 for 24 as England were bowled out for 46. Again and again he did it alongside Courtney Walsh, the partner with whom he shouldered the West Indies attack in the later 1990s.

What made him special

Height, pace and precision. From so high up, the ball reared from a full length, and he hardly ever gave batsmen anything loose; on the rare occasions he did, he was known to scold himself for it. He saved his best for the best players, and Mike Atherton was the man he dismissed more often than any other.

His batting was more modest, at 12.41 an innings, though he did make one Test fifty against Australia in 1991. For years he was famously reluctant to talk to reporters, although he became a good deal more chatty once he had retired.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1992. When he came out to bat in his last Test, in England in 2000, the home side lined up to clap him to the crease. After retiring he was elected to the ICC Hall of Fame, and in 2014 Antigua and Barbuda made him a knight of its Order of the Nation, on the same day as Richie Richardson and Andy Roberts. In 2022 he became bowling coach of the Jamaica Tallawahs.

And finally

After cricket he turned to music, playing bass guitar for a reggae outfit called Big Bad Dread and the Baldhead, with his old team-mate Richardson in the line-up too. A man who spent twelve years refusing to give runs away turned out to have plenty of rhythm to spare.
